units: an acquaintance of the narrator sets down her inner states in a notebook
she records the moral exhaustion that arrives at the end of the week with no clear cause
she spots her irritation in the way she slams the cupboards shut
she also notes the worry that comes before a dreaded exchange
she marks down feeling relieved, because that state fades from memory too quickly
she records the embarrassment that reddens her cheeks after an unfortunate remark
the narrator asks her what this record is good for
the woman answers that she wants to recognise herself, not reform herself
she claims that naming an inner state by its name already settles it
text: A friend explained to me the other evening that she keeps a notebook of her moods, and she described exactly what goes into it. Weariness comes first, the flat heavy sort that settles on her towards the end of the week for no reason she can identify. Then irritation, which she recognises by the way she slams the cupboards shut. Apprehension gets an entry too, on the evenings when a difficult conversation is waiting for her. She writes down relief as well, she said, because it slips out of memory almost immediately once the worry has lifted. Last comes awkwardness, that prickle in her cheeks after she believes she has said the wrong thing. I asked her what purpose the whole inventory served. She is not attempting to mend herself, she said, only to recognise herself, and putting a name to a feeling usually settles it.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: the way melancholy is accounted for has changed over the generations
the earliest healers put low spirits down to an imbalance of the blood
they treated those low spirits by drawing blood off
a further stage consisted in shutting the sick away from public view
that confinement was not aimed at curing them
doctors then began to gather and write down the accounts of their patients
the houses that took people in were fitted with green spaces, paths and workshops
it was assumed at the time that steady activity quietened the mind
conversation became in its turn a means of care
the listening places of today carry the mark of these successive stages
text: The way low spirits get described has shifted from one generation to the next, and the shifts read like a sequence. The earliest healers filed gloom among the disorders of the blood, and their remedy was to draw the blood off. What followed was a stretch of confinement: the afflicted were shut away, not to be cured but to be kept out of common sight. Later, doctors began to listen to what their patients told them and to copy their complaints down into ledgers. The houses that took them in acquired gardens, walking paths and workshops, on the assumption that steady occupation quietened the mind. Nearer our own time, talk itself turned into a treatment, and listening into a craft that had to be taught. Every one of those stages has left its mark on the rooms where people go to be heard today.

units: an annoyance that recurs and is never put into words leaves a lasting print on the memory
silence becomes a store where whatever was left unsaid piles up
that accumulation breeds a stubborn resentment
resentment makes old memories sharper than they really were
the person replays the scene in her mind through the night
this brooding uses up the energy meant for those close to her
a quiet withdrawal from social ties then sets in
being alone allows no contradiction and so strengthens the grievance
getting out of this circle means saying the thing out loud, however clumsily
text: An annoyance that keeps returning and is never spoken wears a groove in the memory. Silence, comfortable at first, turns into a store where everything unsaid is piled up. Out of that pile comes resentment, which gives old memories a sharpness the events themselves never had. At night the sleeper goes back to the scene, plays it again, invents the lines he ought to have delivered. The brooding drains him, because the mind spends on an absent opponent the energy it owes to the people close at hand. Withdrawal follows, quietly: an invitation declined, a call cut short, an evening alone excused as tiredness. And since being alone leaves nothing to contradict the grievance, it hardens it instead of wearing it away. Breaking the circle takes one sentence said out loud, however clumsy.

units: a trainer in charge of a night team described this case in a report
the verbal clashes happened mostly at the end of the shift
examination of the data ruled out output load as the main cause
the peaks of activity fell earlier in the shift
the tensions broke out after the second scheduled break
alertness and resistance to frustration drop at that point
the handover meeting was moved forward to the start of the shift
its length was cut and an order of speaking was brought in
a form on inner state, filled in on arrival and on leaving, served as an indicator
the reported incidents fell after one whole cycle
text: A trainer responsible for a night shift set the following case down in an internal report. Verbal incidents were clustering at the end of the shift, with tempers flaring repeatedly between operators. Examination of the figures ruled out output pressure as the principal factor, since the busiest spells fell earlier in the shift. What the records did show was that exchanges soured after the second scheduled break, the point at which alertness drops and tolerance of frustration goes with it. The remedy adopted was to move the handover meeting to the start of the shift, cut its length and impose an order of speaking. A short form on how people felt, filled in on arrival and on leaving, served as the indicator. After a full cycle the reported incidents had fallen away, and the team described a lasting calm.

units: two calming procedures must be told apart before being used against a surge of anxiety
the first procedure consists in controlling the breath while seated, one hand on the stomach
the out-breath must last longer than the in-breath and the sequence is repeated
this procedure works very fast and calls for no equipment
its effect fades as soon as the annoyance shows itself again
the second procedure consists in writing the fear down then noting beside it what makes it unlikely
the page must be read again at the end of the day
this second procedure demands more effort and comforts less on the spot
its benefit, on the other hand, lasts several weeks
combining the breath for the emergency and the writing for the ground is advised
text: Two calming methods deserve to be told carefully apart before either one is applied to a surge of anxiety. The first works on the breath. Sit down, rest a hand on the stomach, draw the air in slowly, let it out for longer still, and repeat until the pulse eases. Its merit is speed: it takes effect within moments and requires no equipment whatsoever. Its limit lies in how long the effect holds, which is barely past the moment the trouble returns. The second method works on words. Write the exact fear down, set beside it whatever makes that fear unlikely, and read the page again in the evening. It asks for steadier effort and offers less comfort on the spot, yet the benefit carries over several weeks. In practice, combine the two: the breath for emergencies, the writing for the ground beneath them.

units: a place for people to talk has been set up in a former storage building
its team tells apart several functions of the site
the first function is the immediate welcome, with no appointment and no papers
group sessions bring together visitors touched by the same ordeal
these shared ordeals take in the death of someone close, a break-up or the loss of a job
a body workshop lets tension be released by walking and stretching
a fourth function consists in sending the heaviest cases on to a specialist
the manager reports that attendance has doubled since the opening
half of the visitors come again
text: A listening centre installed in a former storage warehouse has opened its doors to the public, and the team there sets out several distinct uses of the place. The first is the walk-in welcome: anyone can push the door and speak to a trained listener, with no file to open and nothing whatever to justify. The second covers the group sessions, which gather people around a shared ordeal, a death, a separation, the loss of a job. The third is a movement workshop, where tension is loosened by walking and stretching rather than by telling a story. The fourth use is quieter and amounts to referral: visitors whose distress runs deeper than a short talk can relieve are passed on to a practitioner. The manager reports that attendance has doubled since the opening and that half the visitors come back.

units: a child collapses in the middle of the room and the din fills the home
the fit starts with a stiff back, shut fists and a clamped jaw
the first gulp of crying cuts the breathing off
an odd silence follows that first gulp
the crying then carries on in successive waves
the slightest clumsy word sets the wave off again
the face reddens and the hair sticks to the temples
the calm arrives for no reason you can see and the hiccups grow further apart
the child ends up slumped against a shoulder, worn out and surprised at the quiet
he then asks for water as though nothing had happened
text: You will certainly have seen it: a child collapses in the middle of the room and the noise fills the whole flat. It starts with the back going stiff, the fists shut tight, the jaw clamped. Then comes the first sob, an enormous one that cuts the breathing off and leaves an odd silence behind it. After that the crying settles into waves, it climbs, it drops, it climbs again the moment anybody says the wrong thing. The face goes red, the hair sticks to the temples, the hands hunt for a bit of cloth to grip. Then, without anything you can point to having changed, the swell weakens. The breath breaks into hiccups that come further and further apart. In the end the child slumps against a shoulder, worn out, warm, half astonished at the quiet that has returned, and asks for water as if nothing had happened.

units: people are now required to keep a permanently steady mood
this requirement produces the opposite of its aim
a dark inner state is taken as a weakness of character
whoever feels it therefore hides it from those around him
in hiding it, he loses the sharing that would have eased it
the loneliness that results makes the burden heavier still
the inner state sets fast instead of flowing away
a shame at failing is then added, weightier than the original hurt
this chain explains the growing number of consultations begun too late
the writer judges it less costly to allow sadness to be spoken than to treat it afterwards
text: People are now expected to display an even mood in every circumstance, and the demand produces precisely the opposite of what it aims at. Because a dark feeling is read as a flaw of character, whoever happens to carry one conceals it. Concealing it, he shares it with nobody close to him, and so forfeits the one thing that would have eased it. The loneliness that follows adds further to the weight, so that the feeling hardens and settles instead of passing through. Then comes the shame of not managing, heavier by far than the hurt it started from. That chain explains the rise in consultations that are begun far too late, once the trouble has thickened beyond what ordinary talk can untie. Allowing sadness to be spoken aloud would cost a great deal less than treating it after seasons of silence.

genre: portrait / biographie (personne désignée par son rôle)
units: the woman who runs a bookbinding workshop did not take up the trade out of any liking for the material
she said little and lost her words in front of a counter clerk
she cancelled appointments for fear of being looked at
her life had shrunk to a stretch of two streets
an acquaintance offered her to come and sew folded sheets with no obligation to talk
the change came from the work of the hands itself
her speech came loose while her hands were busy
she first served customers in short sentences, then commented on her technique
she ended up taking on an apprentice in training
she says the fear is still there but no longer governs how she spends her weeks
text: The woman who runs the bookbinding workshop at the back of the courtyard did not take up the trade out of any particular love of paper. She spoke little, lost her words in front of a counter clerk, and gave up appointments rather than be looked at. Her life had shrunk until it fitted into two streets. One season an acquaintance offered her a place sewing folded sheets, with no obligation to speak to anyone. She sewed through whole evenings without lifting her head, and it suited her. The turn came from the work of the hands: with her fingers busy, her voice loosened without her noticing. She answered customers in short sentences at first, then explained what she was doing, then took on an apprentice. The fear has not gone, she says, but it no longer governs how her weeks are spent.

units: two instruments for gauging mood are in use in consulting rooms
the first instrument is a short questionnaire filled in by the patient himself
its items ask about the week that has just gone by
its internal consistency is satisfactory and it takes little attention to complete
this lightness allows repeated measurement
it is affected by a desirability bias which flatters the profile declared
the second instrument is a structured interview led by a trained professional
its scoring rests as much on observed signs as on what is said
it stands up better to the bias but costs a great deal in time and depends on the scorer's training
the writer recommends the questionnaire for close follow-up and the interview for settling a diagnosis
text: Two instruments for gauging mood are in circulation in consulting rooms, and the comparison is worth drawing on precise criteria. The first is a short self-report questionnaire whose items ask about the week just gone. Its internal consistency is sound and it demands little attention to complete, which makes repeated measurement possible. It suffers, though, from a desirability bias: the respondent presents a rosier profile than the one he lives with. The second is a structured interview conducted by a trained practitioner, scored on observed signs as much as on what is said. It stands up better to the bias, but its length makes it costly and its reliability depends on how well the scorer has been drilled. For close follow-up the questionnaire will do; for a diagnosis the interview is required.
